items.title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
items.summary: This post shows how to use Crawl4AI, an open source web crawler, as a content preparation layer for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, handling JavaScript rendering, selective extraction, and custom metadata enrichment before web content reaches an Amazon S3 data source.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI

 When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default.

 For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content.

 Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source.

 In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation.

 This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova.

 Solution overview

 Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content.

 Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion:

 Structured Markdown preparation : Use DefaultMarkdownGenerator with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites.

 Bounded, targeted extraction : Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns.

 Custom metadata : Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them.

 Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs.

 The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

 By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. The following diagram shows the Crawl4AI path from the schedule through to retrieval.

 Figure 1: The Crawl4AI-to-Amazon S3 ingestion path for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

 The numbered steps in the diagram map to the following workflow:

 Amazon EventBridge starts the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate on the configured schedule.

 The task crawls the public websites you configured and prepares Markdown with a metadata sidecar for each page.

 The task uploads the prepared files to the Amazon S3 bucket that backs the knowledge base data source.

 The task starts an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion job.

 Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases reads the new and changed objects, parses them, and applies the chunking strategy you selected.

 It creates embeddings and indexes them in the knowledge base’s vector store, which Amazon Bedrock manages for a managed knowledge base.

 Your generative AI application queries the knowledge base for relevant chunks or for a generated response with citations.

 The task reads its non-secret pipeline configuration from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store at startup.

 The workflow processes public pages only and doesn’t implement authenticated sessions. For sites that require sign-in, evaluate the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler authentication options first, which include basic, form-based, and SAML authentication. Extending the sample with authentication requires session handling, credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, and a security review.

 How the workflow works

 The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app packages the implementation in a container image during deployment. When the schedule fires, the container runs scripts/container_entrypoint.py and executes crawl, upload, and ingestion in sequence. The following three steps explain the core logic.

 Step 1: Crawl and extract content

 The crawl step performs bounded crawling and writes a Markdown file with a metadata sidecar for each successfully prepared page. The following excerpt is simplified. The module src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/crawl.py contains the complete seed pacing, URL filtering and scoping, page limits, and redirect checks:

 async def crawl_and_prepare(config: PipelineConfig, output_dir: str) -> list[str]:
 written, seen = [], set()
 pages_crawled = 0
 browser_config = BrowserConfig(headless=True, java_script_enabled=True)

 async with AsyncWebCrawler(config=browser_config) as crawler:
 for seed in config.seed_urls:
 remaining = config.crawl.max_pages - pages_crawled
 if remaining <= 0:
 break

 strategy = BFSDeepCrawlStrategy(
 max_depth=config.crawl.max_depth,
 max_pages=remaining,
 filter_chain=FilterChain([
 SeedScopeFilter(seed, config.crawl.scope),
 # Optional include/exclude URLPatternFilter objects are added here.
 ]),
 )
 run_config = CrawlerRunConfig(
 deep_crawl_strategy=strategy,
 markdown_generator=DefaultMarkdownGenerator(
 content_filter=PruningContentFilter()
 ),
 css_selector=config.crawl.css_selector, # Optional page region.
 check_robots_txt=config.crawl.check_robots_txt,
 mean_delay=config.crawl.request_delay_seconds,
 max_range=0,
 semaphore_count=1,
 )

 results = await crawler.arun(url=seed, config=run_config)
 for result in results:
 if pages_crawled >= config.crawl.max_pages:
 break
 pages_crawled += 1
 requested_url = result.url
 source_url = getattr(result, "redirected_url", None) or requested_url
 if not SeedScopeFilter(seed, config.crawl.scope).apply(source_url):
 continue # Recheck the effective destination after redirects.
 canonical = _canonical_url(source_url)
 if canonical in seen:
 continue
 seen.add(canonical)
 if not result.success or not result.markdown:
 continue

 md_result = result.markdown
 markdown = (
 getattr(md_result, "fit_markdown", None)
 or getattr(md_result, "raw_markdown", None)
 or (md_result if isinstance(md_result, str) else "")
 )
 if not markdown:
 continue

 # The complete implementation adds title, crawl timestamps, content
 # type, and configured custom attributes to this metadata.
 written.extend(
 _write_document(
 output_dir,
 _base_name(source_url),
 markdown,
 {"source_url": source_url},
 )
 )
 return written 

 Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports several document formats for Amazon S3 data sources, including plain text, HTML, Markdown, PDF, and DOCX. The workflow writes Markdown because it preserves headings, lists, and tables without carrying all raw HTML into ingestion.

 Step 2: Upload to Amazon S3

 The upload step sends each prepared Markdown document and its matching metadata sidecar to the configured S3 bucket, under the workflow’s s3Prefix . For page.md , the sidecar must be named page.md.metadata.json , the complete source filename with .metadata.json appended. The workflow stores each sidecar in the same S3 location as its document. Amazon Bedrock limits each metadata sidecar to 10 KB. If a sidecar would exceed that limit, the run stops with an error before it writes either file.

 Each attribute in the sidecar uses the typed format that both managed and customer-managed knowledge bases accept for Amazon S3 data sources. The following abbreviated sidecar, formatted for readability, shows three of the attributes that the workflow writes:

 {
 "metadataAttributes": {
 "source_url": {
 "value": {"type": "STRING", "stringValue": "https://www.example.com/services/permits"}
 },
 "crawled_at_epoch": {
 "value": {"type": "NUMBER", "numberValue": 1790640000}
 },
 "content_category": {
 "value": {"type": "STRING", "stringValue": "web"}
 }
 }
} 

 The pipeline uploads only the paths produced by the current crawl, so stale local files are not sent.

 Step 3: Let Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunk, embed, and index

 After content is in S3, an ingestion job hands each document to the data source’s ingestion pipeline. By default, a managed knowledge base parses each file with its managed parser, which automatically selects a parsing approach for your content. You select the chunking strategy when you connect the data source. You can’t change it afterward, so evaluate the options before you create a production data source. A managed know

items.title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
items.summary: Agentic assistants built on frontier models run a multi-step tool loop, and paying frontier prices on every step is hard to sustain at production scale. This post shows how to use sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD) to transfer a frontier teacher's agentic behavior into a small, lower-cost student on Amazon SageMaker AI.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI

 You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping.

 One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost.

 In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark.

 Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper

 What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)?

 The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data.

 In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces.

 For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself.

 Figure 2: SeqKD transfers behavior through the teacher’s text outputs alone: the teacher generates trajectories, the student trains on them, and the result keeps much of the teacher’s quality at the small model’s speed and cost. No teacher weights, logits, or gradients are required during training, so it runs as ordinary supervised fine-tuning

 When SeqKD is the right choice

 SeqKD fits a specific set of situations:

 You have the inputs but no high-quality target outputs 

 This is the core case for SeqKD, which is fundamentally data generation. You supply the inputs, and the teacher writes the targets, so you can fine-tune on a task or domain that has no existing high-quality labels. The targets can be as simple as single answers or as involved as multi-turn tool-use trajectories. This post takes the demanding end of that spectrum, agentic trajectories, which are especially hard to source. A single task branches into many partially correct runs, and telling a solved run from a failed one takes a reliable grader. A benchmark with a programmatic scorer supplies exactly that, so you can let the teacher generate trajectories and keep only the ones that solve the task.

 Your teacher is a frontier model you can only reach through an API 

 This is the normal case for frontier models. You can’t access the weights to host it yourself, you can’t read its logits, and you can’t fine-tune it. That rules out logit-based distillation and on-policy methods, which all need that internal access. SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text responses, so it is the one approach that still works, and it frees you from paying frontier prices on every request after the student takes over.

 You want a strong, cost-effective first step 

 Some of the strongest small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD (supervised fine-tuning on teacher reasoning traces), so it is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are a well-known example: the reasoning of a large teacher was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students by fine-tuning them on the teacher’s generated reasoning traces.

 Prerequisites

 To run this example, you need:

 An AWS account with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for SageMaker AI that has read and write access to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and permission to invoke your teacher model.

 A frontier teacher model to generate the trajectories (this walkthrough uses one on Amazon Bedrock ).

 Access to SageMaker AI model customization in a supported AWS Region.

 Amazon SageMaker Studio (or a local IDE with the AWS CLI configured ), running a Python 3.12 or higher kernel, with the SageMaker Python SDK v3 and boto3 (pin your versions). Use an ml.m5.4xlarge instance at minimum for the notebook environment, since the data preparation and local scoring steps run on its CPU.

 Working knowledge of Python, supervised fine-tuning, and tool-using agents.

 The accompanying code repository and a task with a programmatic scorer (this walkthrough uses the ShoppingBench test set. Substitute your own task and grader).

 Solution overview

 This section walks the pipeline from end to end. A frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock, acts as the ShoppingBench agent to generate trajectories. The benchmark’s own scorer keeps only the ones that solve the task, and those solved trajectories fine-tune a Qwen3.5-4B student with serverless supervised fine-tuning on SageMaker AI model customization. The distilled student is then evaluated on a held-out ShoppingBench split and served behind a SageMaker AI Inference real-time endpoint that runs the tool loop.

 Figure 3: Distilling a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI: a frontier teacher on Amazon Bedrock acts as the ShoppingBench agent on the training problems, ShoppingBench’s own scorer keeps only the trajectories that solve the task (rejection sampling), each solved trajectory is encoded per step, the student is fine-tuned serverlessly with Amazon SageMaker AI model customization, and the result is evaluated on the held-out ShoppingBench test split

 Preparing the dataset

 Sourcing trajectories worth imitating is the hard part, and the ShoppingBench scorer is what separates the successful runs from the failed ones. ShoppingBench publishes 750 synthesized shopping problems, 250 each for the product, shop, and voucher intents, each with a hidden gold answer and the constraints that define success. We split them once into 426 training problems and 324 held-out evaluation problems (product 103, shop 105, voucher 116), as fixed indices so the two sets don’t overlap.

 For each training problem, a frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock with reasoning on and temperature 1.0, acts as the ShoppingBench agent. It searches the catalog of about 2.7 million products, inspects candidates, and recommends the ones that meet the constraints. We sample the teacher twice per problem, which gives 850 trajectories, then let ShoppingBench’s own scorer keep only the ones that solve the task. Temperature 1.0 is deliberate. Sampling rather than greedy decoding makes the two attempts explore different queries and reasoning paths, which gives more problems at least one solved trajectory and a more diverse set to learn from. This rejection-sampling step turns a capable-but-imperfect teacher into a clean training set, since the teacher only has to be right often enough that the solved runs are worth imitating.

 Each solved trajectory is a complete episode: the shopper request, the teacher’s reasoning and tool calls at each step (search, inspect, recommend, terminate), and the observation the environment returned. We keep the reasoning alongside the actions, which the Results show is what carries the student most of the way to its teacher.

 Encoding trajectories for training

 Sequence-level distillation is supervised learning over trajectories that already exist, so nothing calls a tool during training, and the application only ever sees text. Because these trajectories are multi-step tool-use conversations, we encode each as a messages list of chat turns and let the student’s own chat template render it, so the tokens the trainer sees match the tokens the agent produce

items.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: Learn how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that compresses aerospace component substitution evaluation from days to minutes, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the Strands Agents SDK to assemble substitution evidence while keeping the engineer as the decision-maker.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check.

 A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment.

 In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own.

 Solution overview

 The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead.

 Three pillars define the architecture:

 Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review.

 Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence.

 Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6.

 The following diagram shows the architecture.

 Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document.

 Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles:

 Multimodal retrieval – Datasheets, ICDs, and performance charts are embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings so text and visual content share one semantic space. An engineer can enter “torque curve for the 0.06 Nms wheel” or upload a chart image, and retrieval returns the matching diagram with source attribution.

 Visual similarity scoring – When two candidate parts are compared, Nova Multimodal Embeddings produces a quantitative cosine similarity between their photos, and Claude analyzes the specific physical differences (mounting pattern, connector placement, housing geometry). The score adds supporting evidence to the deterministic spec comparison, which is what the fit verdict is based on.

 Prerequisites

 To follow along, you need:

 An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region.

 Model access to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

 A managed knowledge base created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings over your parts corpus (datasheets, ICDs, descriptions) for text and document retrieval.

 An Amazon S3 Vectors index over your part photos and datasheet chart crops, for the image-as-query path.

 An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector and a managed knowledge base target.

 Python 3.10 or later and Jupyter for running the notebooks.

 Docker, if you adapt the deployment recipe in notebook 03 to host the agent on AgentCore runtime.

 The sample code from the GitHub repository .

 Solution walkthrough

 The following sections describe each part of the system in the order a query uses it. We start with the parts corpus and the specialist agents, then cover routing, deterministic scoring, the two ways the assistant uses Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the fixed chain that produces formal documents, and deployment to AgentCore runtime.

 The complete code sample is a set of five Jupyter notebooks in the GitHub repository , and each notebook runs on its own. The notebooks import from mei_core , a self-contained copy of the agent and tool modules in the same folder, and they include their own parts data, chart crops, and evaluation query set. You can run every snippet in this post from the notebooks without other application code.

 Structure the parts corpus

 The sample dataset is seven reaction wheels from a fictional manufacturer (AnyCompany) spanning 0.003–5.0 Nms of momentum storage. Each part is a folder that pairs structured data with the source documents an engineer actually reads, and this mix is what makes the corpus multimodal. The specs.json file holds the machine-readable fields that drive deterministic scoring, while the ICD, product photo, and rendered datasheet page carry the visual and narrative detail that structured fields leave out.

 data/synthetic-parts-data/rw_rl_0060/
├── specs.json # structured specs + lifecycle fields
├── description.txt # flat text for text retrieval
├── AC-ICD-00068-RW3-0.06-Interface-Control-Document-v2.2.pdf
├── datasheet_page.png # rendered datasheet page
├── datasheet_chart.png # cropped chart region (image-as-query index)
└── photo.png # product image (visual similarity + chart matching) 

 The specs.json file captures both the engineering specifications and a lifecycle profile, which is what lets the assistant flag obsolescence and lead-time risk alongside spec fit.

 {
 "name": "AnyCompany RW3 0.06",
 "category": "reaction_wheel",
 "vendor": "AnyCompany",
 "model": "RW3-0.06",
 "momentum_storage_nms": 0.06,
 "max_torque_mnm": 20,
 "mass_g": 235,
 "voltage_v": "28",
 "voltage_range_v": "7.5 to 36",
 "operating_temp_c": "-30 to +70",
 "interface": "RS-422 or Redundant RS-485",
 "qual_standard": "AnyCompany internal (flight heritage qualified)",
 "lifecycle": {
 "lifecycle_status": "Active",
 "production_status": "Full production",
 "estimated_years_to_eol": "10+",
 "last_time_buy": "Not announced",
 "typical_lead_time_weeks": 10,
 "lead_time_risk": "Low",
 "bathtub_region": "Useful life (highly mature)",
 "recommended_screening": "Standard flight acceptance"
 }
} 

 The vendor field is stated explicitly for every part. Because catalog folder IDs and file names are reused across datasets, every specialist prompt treats the structured vendor value returned by get_part_specs as authoritative and is forbidden from guessing a manufacturer from an ID, a file name, a photo, or a web search result. Taking the manufacturer from structured data keeps the assistant from attributing a part to the wrong supplier because the model thinks it recognizes the hardware.

 Each part folder also carries two assets that text-only indexing cannot use. The product photo feeds visual similarity scoring, and the rendered datasheet page carries torque-box and torque-curve plots that answer performance questions no OCR text layer captures. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds both into the same vector space as the text, so a query can match a spec value, a paragraph, or a plot.

 The following sample shows four datasheet pages from the corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage.

 Figure 2: Four datasheet pages from the parts corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage

 The template repeats across the family, but the product photo and the pair of performance plots change with every part. These Regions show the housing geometry, mounting pattern, torque envelope, and power draw, which the spec fields don’t state

items.title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Circle K's DevOps team cut incident triage from 45-60 minutes to under 15 by building an agentic triage system on Amazon Bedrock. This post walks through the architecture, the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation, the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the lessons learned from scaling it.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock

 This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. 

 Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin.

 At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin.

 To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened.

 Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics.

 In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system.

 The challenge of triage overhead

 Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context.

 When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service , checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded.

 The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently.

 Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation.

 Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock

 The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls.

 With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. They could access foundation models through a single API and swap foundation models without rewriting code. Because Circle K already ran on AWS, Amazon Bedrock fit into existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations, and logging pipelines.

 Two managed capabilities covered orchestration and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock helped with agent orchestration, giving the agents native tool use to call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents without custom orchestration code. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handled ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards, so the team did not need to run a separate vector database. This let the DevOps team focus on prompt design and tool definitions.

 Data privacy completed the picture. Circle K’s incident data includes operational metrics, infrastructure details, and logs that can contain sensitive information. Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers or use it to train foundation models . For a team feeding production logs and internal service details into the system, this data handling approach met Circle K’s security requirements.

 Solution overview

 This section describes the initial architecture, which the team built on Amazon Bedrock Flows. A later section covers the migration to AgentCore.

 The solution uses Amazon Bedrock Flows as the orchestration layer, coordinating a set of specialized agents that each handle a different part of the analysis. The pipeline starts when a Grafana alert publishes a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) , which forwards it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function polls the queue, extracts the alert payload, and invokes the Flow.

 Inside the Flow, two agents are invoked in parallel. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent queries infrastructure across multiple workload accounts managed with AWS Organizations . It checks Amazon ECS task status, Application Load Balancer target health, and CloudWatch metrics and logs. At the same time, the OpenSearchExplorerAgent queries Amazon OpenSearch Service for application-level logs and distributed traces. This agent runs separately because OpenSearch returns large volumes of log data. Isolating it keeps each agent’s context window manageable. It also has exclusive access to the knowledge base, which contains product cards describing each service and its dependencies.

 After both agents return their findings, the GitHubExplorerAgent runs. It receives output from the previous two agents and finds the affected service’s GitHub repositories. Then it searches their application code, infrastructure definitions, and recent commits to pinpoint the source of the problem and propose a concrete fix. Running it after the parallel agents means it knows exactly what to search for rather than performing a broad query.

 All three outputs feed into an AnalysisPrompt node, which is a single model call with no tools attached. It receives the AWS resource data, the OpenSearch logs, and the GitHub context, then produces a structured summary: probable root cause, supporting evidence, affected service and owner, and recommended remediation steps. The prompt output uses a consistent format that the on-call team can scan in under 2 minutes.

 The Flow returns this summary to the invoking Lambda function, which posts it to a Slack channel. The entire process from alert to Slack message takes 5–15 minutes depending on incident complexity.

 The following diagram shows this architecture end to end, from the initial Grafana alert to the final Slack summary.

 Figure 1: Circle K automated incident triage architecture using Amazon Bedrock Flows

 Example triage

 A Grafana alert: HTTP 5xx error rate on a service exceeds 5% for 3 consecutive minutes.

 The AWSResourceExplorerAgent checks ECS task health in the target account and finds the database connection pool exhausted, with the ECS service attempting restarts. The OpenSearchExplorerAgent returns application logs showing “connection refused” errors from the service to its backing PostgreSQL database. It also retrieves the product card for the affected service from the knowledge base, which documents its dependency on that database. The GitHubExplorerAgent searches the service’s repository and infrastructure files and finds the Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) definition. It sees that the service opens a new database connection per request rather than reusing existing ones.

 The AnalysisPrompt receives all three results. It correlates the timing with a scheduled marketing campaign that started 10 minutes before the alert. It combines that with the GitHubExplorerAgent’s finding to recommend a concrete code-level fix rather than a temporary patch.

 The final Slack message reads:

 Summary: XYZ Service 5xx errors caused by connection pool exhaustion
Root cause: Scheduled marketing campaign drove traffic spike; connection pool max (50) insufficient for load
Evidence: OpenSearch logs show "connection refused" at 14:32 UTC; ECS shows 3 task restarts since 14:30
Owner: XYZ team (backend)
Next steps: Add Amazon RDS Proxy to pool connections, or update the service to reuse existing connections instead of opening a new one per request; consider an Auto Scaling rule for future campaigns 

 Scaling to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 The Amazon Bedrock Flows architecture worked well for months, and simple incidents were triaged in under 10 minutes. Over time, the volume of data and the context behind each investigation grew, even though the set of services stayed the same. Some incidents required longer-running analysis than a single Flow node could complete.

 The team first optimized within the existing design by filtering logs more aggressively, shortening context windows, and splitting certain services int

items.content:
research area Human-Computer Interaction , research area Methods and Algorithms 

 content type paper published November 2026 
 Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live iOS Apps

 Authors Peitong Duan*, Seyed Khashaiar Gatmiry*, Jeff Nichols, Emmanuel Abbe, Samy Bengio

 View publication 
 Copy Bibtex 

 While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
 * Equal contribution

 Related readings and updates.

many perform poorly on UI tasks due to the lack of UI training data. In this paper, we adapt a recipe for generating paired text-image
training data for VLMs to the UI domain by combining existing pixel-based methods with a Large Language Model (LLM). Unlike
prior art, our method requires no human-provided annotations,â¦

Simulation / Modeling / Design 

 Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos

 Nov 02, 2026

 By Pranjali Joshi , Aditya Mahajan , Wonsik Han , Saeed Babamohamadi and Mostafa Toloui 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA Cosmos provides world foundation models and development tools for physical AI, addressing sensor adaptation and reliable deployment challenges.
 Cosmos Framework offers modular, open tools for training, reinforcement learning, optimization, and inference across models including Cosmos 3, NVIDIA Alpamayo, GR00T, Qwen, and pi0.5.
 Cosmos 3 Nano simulation recipes generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR observations for autonomous vehicle, robotics, and surgical scenarios using released checkpoints.
 Cosmos NIM microservices deliver accelerated inference with quantization, speculative decoding, and KV-cache-aware routing, achieving roughly 2–3x speedups on H200 GPUs.
 GPU memory requirements vary by model and task, with Cosmos3-Nano generation needing 58 GiB in BF16 and 44 GiB in FP8 with offloading.
 Next Steps
 Explore the Cosmos Framework to train, customize, and optimize models for your application.
 Read the full technical report for detailed methodology and results.
 Watch the livestream on Thursday, Nov. 5 to learn how to use Cosmos Framework.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 Physical AI developers working with world models face two distinct challenges: adapting models to their sensors, tasks, and data, and getting those models into applications reliably. 

 NVIDIA Cosmos addresses each. Cosmos is a platform of world foundation models and development tools for physical AI . Cosmos Framework provides agent skills and recipes for world model training, multimodal data processing, optimization and inference. Cosmos NIM microservices supports GPU-accelerated serving through application APIs.

 This post walks through both. The simulation section shows how to use Cosmos Framework’s inference recipes and agent skills to generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR observations for AV, robot, and surgical scenarios, starting from released checkpoints you can run today. The deployment section shows how to choose a NIM configuration for your GPU, launch the container, verify readiness, and send your first inference request. 

 When to use Cosmos Framework for world model development 

 Cosmos Framework is an open and fully modular framework for world model training, model optimization, and inference to support a full model development lifecycle using new agent skills. It is expanding beyond Cosmos 3 to support NVIDIA Alpamayo , GR00T, Qwen, pi0.5, and other compatible Hugging Face models.

 Training 

 Train models on text, images, video, audio, and actions faster using new skills.

 Use LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation, or full supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to update all model parameters. 

 Load data through JSONL, WebDataset, LeRobot, or custom adapters and train across GPUs and save checkpoints to resume runs.

 Point your agent to post-training skill to accelerate and automate.

 Apply Reinforcement Learning 

 The platform now covers online and offline RL paths . Newly supported pipelines include:

 DPO: offline preference optimization.

 GRPO: online RL with a rule or model reward and vLLM rollouts.

 PPO: actor-critic RL with frozen reference and critic, including RL for embodied policies in simulation.

 OPD: on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher.

 DiffusionNFT: online RL for diffusion world models.

 Run rollout, reward, and training roles on shared GPUs or separate pools.

 Connect supported simulators to collect experience.

 Optimize models and inference 

 Distill models to reduce model size or generation steps; quantize models to reduce memory use.

 Run compatible checkpoints with Hugging Face Diffusers, PyTorch, SGLang, vLLM-Omni, vLLM, TRT-LLM and TRT-Edge-LLM or NVIDIA NIM.

 Evaluate for quality, accuracy and GPU usage and maximize compute utilization.

 Use agents with Cosmos Framework 

 Load the setup, inference, post-training, and troubleshooting skills under .agents/skills . Give the agent a bounded task:

 Prompt : Post-train <checkpoint> on <dataset> using <recipe> . Pin all revisions, validate the dataset, and keep training and evaluation episodes separate. Run the smoke test, save the configuration, and stop at <N> GPU-hours. Export and compare against the base model on held-out data using three seeds. Repeat evaluation at a supported lower precision; record quality, peak memory, and latency. 

 Which Cosmos simulation workflow should you use? 

 Cosmos Framework provides post-training and inference recipes for robot simulation, realistic scene generation, multi-camera driving simulation, and surgical policy evaluation. New Cosmos 3 Nano simulation recipes and example checkpoints enable developers to use agent runnable skills to evaluate our example checkpoints and adapt Cosmos 3 Nano to custom sensors, action space, and data domains. 

 These checkpoints support PyTorch and vLLM-Omni, tested on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs. Use the recipe to select GPU count, memory configuration, and inference settings.

 Autonomous vehicle simulation: 

 Both AV checkpoints take a prompt and World Scenario Map (WSM) controls representing lanes, objects, road markings, traffic signs, and road boundaries. Joint RGB–LiDAR generation additionally uses HD-map rangemap controls and supports optional initial LiDAR observations. Prompts describe weather, lighting, time of day, road conditions with prefixes providing camera-rig and field-of-view context. An optional initial camera images provide visual context to guide the generated scene’s appearance. 

 Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto uses bidirectional generation to denoise an entire multi-view clip at once for offline synthetic data generation . It supports 30 fps input and output video, with up to 400 frames at 480p or 720p; longer sequences can be generated through autoregressive chunking. Change the prompt to turn a daytime drive into a rainy night while keeping the same road layout and vehicle trajectories. Use these variations to train and evaluate perception and driving models across weather and lighting conditions.

 After Framework setup, run the four-GPU examples below from the repository root. For Transfer-Auto, use the published sample configuration with seven synchronized WSM videos, per-camera captions, first-frame RGB conditioning, and HD-map LiDAR controls. See the Transfer-Auto inference guide for setup, input preparation, and output details.

export COSMOS_TRAINING=0 COSMOS_INTERNAL=0

hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
 --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT="$PWD/checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto/assets/sample_data"
AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT="$(cat .agents/skills/cosmos3-nano-transfer-auto/inference/assets/negative-prompt.txt)"

torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
 -m cosmos_framework.scripts.inference \
 -i "$AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT/input-transfer-auto.jsonl" \
 -o outputs/transfer_auto \
 --checkpoint-path checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
 --resolution 720 --num-steps 35 \
 --per-view-negative-prompt "$AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT" \
 --cp-size 4 --cfgp-size 1 \
 --no-use-torch-compile --no-diffusion-cache

 The reference run produces seven 720p videos (297 frames at 30 FPS) and 99 LiDAR sweeps. Check sample_outputs.json for success and lidar.safetensors for finite range and intensity values, then verify WSM alignment and consistency across camera views and LiDAR.

 For custom scenarios and rig adaptation, see the WSM renderer and Transfer-Auto post-training guides . For point-cloud conversion and visualization, see the LiDAR visualization utilities 

 Video 1. Surround-view video and LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto 

 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causal, few-step-distilled variant of Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto, enabling autoregressive streaming generation. It generates observations incrementally as an AV policy or human driving input updates the scenario through a WSM renderer. Generated camera and LiDAR observations return to the policy, enabling closed-loop evaluation 

 For Sim-Auto, reproduce the reference rollout using the published Sim-Auto sample checkpoint and pre-rendered WSM controls to generate synchronized camera videos and LiDAR observations autoregressively. See the Sim-Auto inference guide for setup, input configuration, and output details.

 Figure 1. Cosmos closed-loop simulation workflow 

export COSMOS_TRAINING=0 COSMOS_INTERNAL=0

hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto \
 --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
 --include 'assets/sample_data/*' \
 --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT="$PWD/checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto/assets/sample_data"

torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
 -m cosmos_framework.scripts.inference \
 -i "$AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT/input-sim-auto.jsonl" \
 -o outputs/sim_auto \
 --checkpoint-path checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto \
 --cp-size 4 --cfgp-size 1 \
 --no-use-torch-compile --no-diffusion-cache

 For human-controlled rollouts, see Sim-Auto Interactive Drive . 

 The Sim-Auto reference run writes to outputs/sim_auto/daytime_scene/ . Apply the same output checks described above for Transfer-Auto. 

 Video 2. Multi-view video and LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto 

 Robotics Simulation: 

 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer converts depth video and a prompt into RGB video with varied lighting, textures, and backgrounds while preserving geometry and motion. For robot demonstrations, it changes the third-person view while retaining actions, states, and wrist-camera recordings.

 Video 3. Turn depth, segmentation, edges, or blurred video into de

items.content:
Data Center / Cloud 

 Support New AI Frameworks Faster Using NVIDIA Workload Map

 Nov 02, 2026

 By Alon Lavian , Yuval Grauer and Ron Lev 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA Workload Map provides a common Kubernetes workload description that enables schedulers, controllers, and platforms to interpret distributed workloads without framework-specific parsing code.
 The project ships a catalog of prebuilt definitions for JobSet, PyTorchJob, RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, KServe, Knative, MPIJob, NVIDIA NIM, LeaderWorkerSet, Milvus, Grove PodCliqueSet, and NVIDIA Dynamo.
 A single JobSet definition supports workload inspection through the Workload Map CLI, gang scheduling via KAI Scheduler, and unified management in NVIDIA Run:ai.
 Elotl's Nova uses Workload Map to interpret workload structure and resource requirements for multi-cluster scheduling decisions.
 Next Steps
 Explore the workload catalog to find a definition for a framework you already use.
 Join the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Slack workspace to discuss workload definitions and integrations.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, including open source, modular software components built to support multi-tenant operations and scaling.

 Operating an AI factory requires a shared understanding of distributed workloads: their components, pod templates, replica counts, and status. On Kubernetes, each framework encodes that information differently. JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet, and other custom resources often require separate adapters before a tool can interpret and manage them.

 NVIDIA Workload Map provides a common description of Kubernetes workload structure that users can reuse across frameworks. As part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, Workload Map enables integrated schedulers, controllers, and platforms to interpret supported workload types without maintaining separate framework-specific parsing code.

 This post shows how to describe a distributed JobSet workload once, then reuse that definition for workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility.

 Why every workload type needs its own adapter 

 On Kubernetes, a real workload is rarely a single pod. A distributed training job or a multi-node inference server is a small tree of resources: groups of pods, each with a role, a replica count, a pod template, and a status that depends on the workload type.

 Teams building schedulers, controllers, dashboards, or cost tools that must work across these workloads encounter this immediately. The NVIDIA Run:ai team faced the same challenge while creating its platform. For each new custom resource definition (CRD), developers answer the same questions in code:

 What’s the structure of the workload type?

 How is the resource’s status interpreted as a phase?

 How is the pod spec changed without breaking the workload?

 A developer answers those questions once per workload type and produces a per-CRD adapter. Each new framework a customer brings requires another adapter. That makes adapter development a roadmap item per framework, not a one-time cost, which is why support for a new workload type so often waits for a release.

 The following manifest shows a distributed training job as a user submits it: a JobSet with a leader Job and two worker Jobs, each with a pod requesting four GPUs.

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: JobSet
metadata:
 name: demo
spec:
 replicatedJobs:
 - name: leader
 replicas: 1
 template:
 spec:
 parallelism: 1
 completions: 1

 template:
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: leader
 image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest
 resources:
 limits:
 nvidia.com/gpu: 4
 - name: worker
 replicas: 2
 template:
 spec:
 parallelism: 1
 completions: 1

 template:
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: worker
 image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest
 resources:
 limits:
 nvidia.com/gpu: 4

 The manifest describes one leader, two workers, and a total request of 12 GPUs. Interpreting that structure requires JobSet-aware code; kubectl lists the resources separately.

 Figure 1. kubectl lists the demo JobSet, its three Jobs, and their pods as separate resource entries 

$ kubectl get jobset,jobs,pods
NAME TERMINALSTATE RESTARTS COMPLETED SUSPENDED AGE
jobset.jobset.x-k8s.io/demo 0 3m46s

NAME STATUS COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE
job.batch/demo-leader-0 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-0 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-1 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s

NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE
pod/demo-leader-0-0-ksb4l 1/1 Running 0 3m47s
pod/demo-worker-0-0-qv955 1/1 Running 0 3m47s
pod/demo-worker-1-0-5smfn 1/1 Running 0 3m47s

 Owner references connect the Jobs to their JobSet, but a platform still needs a definition to interpret their roles and aggregate resource requests.

 Figure 2. NVIDIA Run:ai displays the component Jobs as three separate workloads, each requesting four GPUs, before the JobSet definition is registered 

 Without a shared workload description, users must reconstruct the workload and total its GPU requests themselves.

 A common description of Kubernetes workload structure 

 Workload Map (formerly Karta; the CRD’s resource kind remains Karta) ships as a Kubernetes CRD plus a Go library that interprets workload definitions. Each definition specifies where to find pod templates, replica counts, and status fields for its workload type.

 Workload Map supplies a shared structural view to scheduling and platform consumers. KAI Scheduler uses its definitions to interpret pod grouping and gang-scheduling instructions, while NVIDIA Run:ai uses them for workload management and visibility. Each consumer acts on the same description, reducing the need for separate framework-specific parsers.

 The Go library resolves a live object into a uniform structural view. With a workload definition in hand, a consumer can:

 Extract pod templates, replica counts, status, and metadata.

 Update pod specs, labels, and annotations across every instance.

 Understand the workload hierarchy, for example, a JobSet’s replicated Jobs and their pods.

 Workload Map includes a catalog of prebuilt, tested definitions for JobSet, PyTorchJob, RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, KServe, Knative, MPIJob, NVIDIA NIM, LeaderWorkerSet, Milvus, Grove PodCliqueSet , and NVIDIA Dynamo . Additional workload types can be added by writing a YAML definition that describes their structure and status.

 The key is that workload knowledge moves out of compiled adapters and into data developers can write, review, and apply to a cluster like any other manifest. The rest of this post describes the JobSet example, then shows how the same definition supports workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility.

 Writing a workload definition for JobSet 

 A workload definition, expressed as a Workload Map resource, describes that shape. The following excerpt shows key parts of the JobSet definition. The full version ships in the repository .

 The root component defines the workload’s own kind and how its status is read.

apiVersion: run.ai/v1alpha1
kind: Karta
spec:
 structureDefinition:
 rootComponent:
 name: jobset
 kind:
 group: jobset.x-k8s.io
 version: v1alpha2
 kind: JobSet
 statusDefinition:
 conditionsDefinition:
 path: .status.conditions
 statusMappings:
 running:
 - byExpression:
 expression: "(.status.replicatedJobsStatus // []) | any(.ready > 0 and .active > 0) and all(.failed == 0)"
 expectedResult: "true"
 completed:
 - byConditions:
 - type: Completed
 status: "True"
 failed:
 - byConditions:
 - type: Failed
 status: "True"

 statusMappings is the translation layer. JobSet does not report a plain “Running” condition, so the definition derives it with a jq expression over replicatedJobsStatus (any Job ready and active, none failed) and maps the native Completed and Failed conditions onto the shared vocabulary a consumer already uses. When a RayJob or a LeaderWorkerSet is described, its very different status maps to the same categories.

 The next excerpt defines the child component: the structure inside the workload.

 childComponents:
 - name: replicatedjob
 kind: { group: batch, version: v1, kind: Job }
 ownerRef: jobset
 specDefinition:
 podTemplateSpecPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].template.spec.template
 scaleDefinition:
 replicasPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[] | .replicas * .template.spec.parallelism
 instanceIdPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].name

 A JobSet declares its roles as a list, so .spec.replicatedJobs holds one entry per role. The [] in these paths means “for each entry in that list,” and each entry is what Workload Map calls an instance. podTemplateSpecPath points to each Job’s pod template. scaleDefinition uses jq : the number of pods per replicated Job equals replicas times parallelism , which is why the example manifest sets parallelism explicitly. instanceIdPath takes each instance’s name from .spec.replicatedJobs[].name , which is how “leader” and “worker” show up as distinct roles instead of three anonymous Jobs.

 Figure 3. Declarative definitions resolve JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet resources into a common workload-tree representation despite their different schemas 

 The framework-specific structure is now captured in one reusable definition. The next section shows how different consumers use it.

 Using one description across tools 

 The same JobSet definition supports three workflows: inspecting workloads, scheduling them together, and managing them as one workload.

 Inspecting workloads with the Workload Map CLI 

 The Workload Map CLI reads workloads from a cluster and renders them through their workload definitions. For the demo JobSet, the CLI loads the JobSet description, resolves the live object and its pods, and prints the tree. The CLI uses a kubeconfig t
